There was an article on /v/news about how a bug was found in OpenSSL allowing hackers to decrypt HTTPS and it prompted me to write out this comment.

Disclaimer: I use GNU/Linux exclusively and free and open source software almost exclusively

Four reasons why FOSS software is not inherently more secure than proprietary:

  1. The code isn't always audited and most amateur and even professional coders are not equipped to do so.
  2. It's nearly impossible to spot a backdoor and even less so if the code is heavily obfuscated.
  3. If you use one of the big distros (Ubuntu, Mint, Debian, etc) you are almost always installing binaries (when running apt-get) and not installing from source. If you don't even have access to the real source code, you cannot even confirm the binary you are installing is compiled from the real source code. Debian/Ubuntu/whatever can slip in a backdoor and you wouldn't even know.
  4. Access to the source makes a hackers job easier. It is much harder with proprietary software, where there is no access to the source code.

Also, accountability. Some coder can slip in a fairly innocuous piece of code that is actually a backdoor and when caught, can claim ignorance. This has happened in the past. Coders and maintainers can be paid off, given NDAs, etc etc.

Not to mention the fact that free software was NEVER intended to be taken that way. Even Linus says he writes the Linux kernel with efficiency in mind and not security.

I really hate this meme that FOSS is inherently secure. Yes, you can look at the source, but have you ever actually done so?

All that being said, I use free software because I don't want to give my data to Microsoft or Apple or Google or whatever, but I am under no illusion that government agencies such as the NSA can steal my data, whether I use Linux or OSX or Windows
Open source software is not inherently more secure than proprietary software. This meme needs to die.

I've been saying this for a long time on Voat.

Some projects are only understandable by it's core maintainers (openssl, systemd) and as such, the "to many eyes, all bugs are shallow" mantra simply doesn't apply.

I still think it's the best model available however.

EDIT: Your point 4 is wrong. What you are relying on by not releasing the source is security through obfuscation, which leads to a false sense of security. A good cracker is quite happy disassembling compiled code and stepping through it in assembler to find those non bounds-checked scanfs. By releasing the source code, researchers can find security flaws before the bad guys in most cases and you win.

8 Deadly Commands You Should Never Run on Linux

Not never for several of them. But you better know what you're doing.

mkfs makes filesystems, this needs to be done on new or repurposed disks.

command > /dev/sda can be used to restore the boot sector for example

dd if=/dev/null of=/dev/sda is an easy way to test the write speed of a disk and to see if the disk has problems. Don't do it on a disk with data though.

dd if=/dev/random of=/dev/sda should be don before a disk is thrown away or given away to make data unrecoverable.
Solid point. Title should probably read "8 Deadly Command Strings You Should never Run on Linux"
